title: Soft-NMS -- Improving Object Detection With One Line of Code
venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)

problem.summary: Greedy non-maximum suppression is a hard-threshold post-processing step that zeroes the scores of neighboring detections, so any object that overlaps the kept box above the threshold is missed, while a fixed threshold tuned for one evaluation overlap degrades average precision at other thresholds.
statements: NMS eliminates any detection overlapping the selected box beyond a fixed threshold, so an object actually present in that overlap region is missed.
NMS applies a hard threshold when deciding what to keep or remove from the neighborhood of the top-scoring box.
Using a low NMS threshold drops average precision when evaluation uses a high overlap criterion, and using a high threshold increases false positives at lower evaluation thresholds.
The NMS component of the detection pipeline has remained untouched for more than a decade.

evidence.quote: As per the design of the algorithm, if an object lies within the predefined overlap threshold, it leads to a miss.
Hence, NMS sets a hard threshold while deciding what should be kept or removed from the neighborhood of M.
Therefore, applying NMS with a low threshold like 0.3 could lead to a drop in average precision when the overlap criterion during evaluation for a true positive is 0.7
Also, using a high Nt like 0.7 would increase false positives when Ot is lower and would hence drop precision averaged over multiple thresholds.

background.summary: The paper situates NMS as a 50-year-old post-processing component of sliding-window and region-proposal detectors, notes prior learning-based and optimization-based alternatives (affinity clustering, proposal subset optimization, QUBO), and argues greedy NMS remains the strongest generic baseline that any replacement must beat without retraining.

evidence.quote: Non-maximum suppression is an integral part of the object detection pipeline.
However, neighboring windows often have correlated scores (which increases false positives), so non-maximum suppression is used as a post-processing step to obtain final detections.
Since there is no constraint in the network which forces it to generate a unique RoI for an object, multiple proposals may correspond to the same object.

solution.summary: Soft-NMS replaces NMS's hard zeroing step with a continuous re-scoring rule: the scores of boxes overlapping the selected box M are decayed by a linear or Gaussian function of their IoU with M, implemented as a one-line change to greedy NMS with no retraining and the same complexity.
solution.approach: Decay the classification scores of overlapping detections as a continuous (linear or Gaussian) function of their IoU with the current top box instead of setting them to zero.
components: linear re-scoring: si = si * (1 - iou(M, bi)) for iou >= Nt
Gaussian re-scoring: si = si * exp(-iou(M, bi)^2 / sigma) for boxes not yet selected
one-line modification of the greedy NMS pseudo-code
no extra training and no change to the detector

evidence.quote: we propose Soft-NMS, an algorithm which decays the detection scores of all other objects as a continuous function of their overlap with M. Hence, no object is eliminated in this process.
Suppose, instead, we decay the classification score of a box bi which has a high overlap with M, rather than suppressing it altogether.
Soft-NMS is a generalized version of non-maximum suppression and traditional NMS is a special case of it with a discontinuous binary weighting function.
Since Soft-NMS does not require any extra training and is simple to implement, it can be easily integrated into any object detection pipeline.

experiments.summary: Soft-NMS is plugged into three off-the-shelf detectors (Faster-RCNN, R-FCN, Deformable-RFCN) and evaluated on PASCAL VOC 2007 test and MS-COCO minival/test-dev with COCO-style AP, plus sensitivity analysis over the NMS threshold and the Gaussian sigma and per-class gain analysis.

evidence.quote: Using Deformable-RFCN, Soft-NMS improves state-of-the-art in object detection from 39.8% to 40.9% with a single model.
Even on PASCAL VOC 2007, Soft-NMS obtains an improvement of 1.7% for both Faster-RCNN and R-FCN.
It is clear that Soft-NMS (using both Gaussian and linear weighting function) improves performance in all cases

limitations.summary: Soft-NMS is still a greedy algorithm that does not reach the globally optimal re-scoring, it introduces a sigma parameter to tune, and its gains are much smaller on non proposal-based detectors such as SSD and YOLOv2; evaluation is limited to PASCAL VOC 2007 and MS-COCO.
items: Soft-NMS remains greedy and does not find the globally optimal re-scoring of detection boxes.
Adds a sigma hyper-parameter that needs tuning (performance varies across sigma values).
Gains shrink to 0.5% for non proposal-based detectors like SSD and YOLOv2.
Only PASCAL VOC 2007 and MS-COCO are evaluated.

evidence.quote: Note that Soft-NMS is also a greedy algorithm and does not find the globally optimal re-scoring of detection boxes.
For detectors like SSD [18] and YOLOv2 [23] which are not proposal based, with the linear function, Soft-NMS only obtains an improvement of 0.5%.
In all our experiments, we set σ to 0.5, even though a σ value of 0.6 seems to give better performance on the coco minival set.

futureDirections.direction: Explore other re-scoring functions beyond linear and Gaussian, such as generalized logistic functions like Gompertz, accepting more hyper-parameters.
futureDirections.quote: Apart from the two proposed functions, other functions with more parameters can also be explored with Soft-NMS which take overlap and detection scores into account.

futureDirections.direction: Try generalized logistic (e.g. Gompertz) weighting functions for Soft-NMS.
futureDirections.quote: For example, instances of the generalized logistic function like the Gompertz function can be used, but such functions would increase the number of hyper-parameters.

deploymentClaims: Computational complexity is the same as traditional NMS (O(N^2) over N detection boxes), so it does not affect detector running time.
At a threshold of 1e-4 with 4 CPU threads it takes 0.01 s per image for 80 classes; at 1e-2, 0.005 s on a single core.
Requires no retraining and can be integrated into any object detection pipeline.

evidence.quote: It has many practical applications in autonomous driving [6, 9], video/image indexing [28, 22], surveillance [2, 11] etc.
Further, the computational complexity of Soft-NMS is the same as traditional NMS and hence it can be efficiently implemented.
At a threshold of 10e-4, using 4 CPU threads, it takes 0.01s per image for 80 classes.
